questions.stem: What causes day and night?
options: The Sun orbiting Earth
The Moon blocking the Sun
Earth rotating on its axis
Earth orbiting the Sun
questions.explanation: One rotation takes about 24 hours. The orbit around the Sun takes a year and causes seasons, not day and night.

questions.stem: How long does Earth take to orbit the Sun once?
options: About one week
About one year
About one day
About one month
questions.explanation: One orbit is a year. One rotation is a day.
questions.teaching:
Earth has two main motions, and each defines a unit of time.

Spinning on its axis produces day and night. Travelling in its orbit around the Sun produces a much longer cycle, and that circuit is what a calendar year measures. Because the orbit takes slightly more than a whole number of days — about a quarter of a day more — an extra day is added every four years to keep the calendar aligned. That leap-year correction is direct evidence of how the two motions relate.

questions.stem: How long does the Moon take to orbit Earth once?
options: About one month
About one day
About one year
About one week
questions.explanation: Roughly 27–29 days, which is where the month comes from.
questions.teaching:
The Moon orbits Earth while Earth orbits the Sun, and the Moon's circuit gives us a familiar unit of time.

One complete orbit takes a little over 27 days, though the cycle of phases we observe takes about 29 and a half — slightly longer, because Earth has moved along its own orbit in the meantime. Either way the period is close to the length of a calendar month, and that is no coincidence: months were originally defined by it, and the word itself is related to 'moon'.

questions.stem: What causes the seasons on Earth?
options: The Moon blocking sunlight
Changes in the Sun's output
The tilt of Earth's axis as it orbits the Sun
Earth being closer to the Sun in summer
questions.explanation: Axial tilt is the cause. Distance is the most common misconception, and the facts run against it: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during the southern hemisphere's summer and the northern hemisphere's winter.

questions.stem: Why does the Moon appear to shine?
options: It produces its own light
It reflects light from Earth
It glows from internal heat
It reflects light from the Sun
questions.explanation: The Moon has no light of its own; we see reflected sunlight.

questions.stem: What is a solar eclipse?
options: The Moon moves behind the Sun
The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, blocking sunlight
Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon
The Sun stops shining briefly
questions.explanation: In a solar eclipse the Moon casts a shadow on Earth. Earth between Sun and Moon gives a lunar eclipse.

questions.stem: What is a lunar eclipse?
options: The Moon stops reflecting light
The Sun passes behind Earth
Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, casting a shadow on it
The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth
questions.explanation: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, which is why a lunar eclipse is visible from the whole night side of Earth.

questions.stem: What mainly causes tides on Earth?
options: The gravitational pull of the Moon
The rotation of the Moon on its axis
Wind blowing across the ocean
Earth's magnetic field
questions.explanation: The Moon's gravity is the main cause, with the Sun contributing a smaller effect.

questions.stem: What is a new moon?
options: When the Moon is in Earth's shadow
When the Moon is closest to Earth
When the Moon's lit side faces away from Earth, so it appears dark
When the Moon is fully lit as seen from Earth
questions.explanation: At new moon the Moon sits roughly between Earth and the Sun, so the lit face points away from us.

questions.stem: What is a full moon?
options: When the Moon is directly overhead
When the whole face of the Moon we see is lit by the Sun
When the Moon is completely dark
When the Moon is closest to Earth
questions.explanation: At full moon Earth sits roughly between the Sun and Moon, so we see the fully lit face.

questions.stem: Which season is it in Australia when the southern hemisphere tilts towards the Sun?
options: Winter
Autumn
Spring
Summer
questions.explanation: Tilting towards the Sun gives more direct sunlight and longer days — summer.
questions.teaching:
Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, not by distance from the Sun — Earth is actually closest to the Sun during the southern summer.

The axis stays pointed the same way as Earth orbits, so for part of the year one hemisphere leans towards the Sun. That hemisphere receives sunlight at a steeper angle, concentrating the energy over a smaller area, and gets longer daylight hours — which together produce its warmest season. Six months later the same hemisphere leans away and gets its coldest. The two hemispheres are therefore always in opposite seasons.

questions.stem: Why is it warmer in summer?
options: The Moon reflects extra heat
Sunlight strikes more directly and days are longer
Earth is much closer to the Sun
The Sun burns hotter
questions.explanation: Angle of sunlight and day length are the causes. Distance is a common wrong answer.

questions.stem: What is the axis of Earth?
options: The line between Earth and the Moon
An imaginary line through the poles that Earth rotates around
The path Earth takes around the Sun
The equator
questions.explanation: The axis is the rotation line. The path around the Sun is the orbit.

questions.stem: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
options: Earth's shadow hides the other side
It rotates once for each orbit of Earth
It does not rotate at all
It is not a sphere
questions.explanation: This is tidal locking: rotation period matches orbital period, so the same face always points towards us.

questions.stem: What is a high tide?
options: When the sea is roughest
When the Moon is full
When the tide stops moving
When sea level at a place is at its highest in the tidal cycle
questions.explanation: Tides are about water level, not wave height or moon phase.

questions.stem: About how often does a coastal place experience high tides?
options: Once a week
Once a month
Roughly twice a day
Once a day
questions.explanation: Most coasts have two high and two low tides in roughly 24 hours and 50 minutes.

questions.stem: Which body is at the centre of our solar system?
options: Earth
The Moon
Jupiter
The Sun
questions.explanation: The Sun is at the centre and the planets orbit it — the heliocentric model.
questions.teaching:
Our solar system is organised around a single central object that holds everything else in orbit.

It contains over 99% of the system's mass, which is why its gravity dominates everything within it. The planets, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets all orbit it, and moons orbit the planets in turn. This arrangement is called heliocentric, and replacing the older Earth-centred model with it was one of the major shifts in the history of science — Copernicus, Galileo and Kepler are the names associated with that change.

questions.stem: What is a crescent moon?
options: When only a thin curved sliver of the lit face is visible
When the Moon is fully lit
When the Moon is completely dark
When the Moon is eclipsed
questions.explanation: A crescent is a small lit fraction, seen near new moon.

questions.stem: Why can eclipses be predicted years in advance?
options: Eclipses happen on the same date every year
The motions of Earth and the Moon are regular and cyclic
Eclipses happen at random
Scientists cause eclipses
questions.explanation: Predictability follows from regular cyclic motion — the point the curriculum makes about modelling these cycles.

questions.stem: Why is a solar eclipse visible from only a small part of Earth?
options: The Moon's shadow covers only a narrow path on Earth's surface
The Sun only disappears in some countries
The Moon is too large to cast a wide shadow
Earth's rotation stops the shadow spreading
questions.explanation: The Moon is small, so its full shadow traces a narrow path. A lunar eclipse, by contrast, is visible from the entire night side.

questions.stem: Why don't we get a solar eclipse every new moon?
options: The Moon is too far away most months
New moons only happen a few times a year
Clouds usually block the view
The Moon's orbit is tilted, so it usually passes above or below the Sun's line
questions.explanation: The roughly five-degree tilt of the Moon's orbit means the three bodies rarely line up exactly.

questions.stem: In the southern hemisphere, when is the longest day of the year?
options: Around late March
Around late September
Around late December
Around late June
questions.explanation: The southern summer solstice falls around 21–22 December, when the south pole tilts most towards the Sun.

questions.stem: Why are the seasons opposite in the northern and southern hemispheres?
options: The hemispheres are different distances from the Sun
Earth rotates in opposite directions in each hemisphere
The Sun heats each hemisphere on alternate years
When one hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, the other tilts away
questions.explanation: One tilt produces two opposite effects at the same moment. Distance would affect both hemispheres equally.

questions.stem: A spring tide is unusually high. What causes it?
options: It only happens during the spring season
Strong winds push water onto the shore
The Moon stops orbiting briefly
The Sun and Moon align so their gravitational pulls combine
questions.explanation: Spring tides occur at new and full moon when the pulls add. The name has nothing to do with the season.

questions.stem: Why does the Moon appear to change shape through the month?
options: We see different fractions of its lit half as it orbits Earth
Earth's shadow covers different amounts of it
The Moon physically changes shape
Clouds cover part of it
questions.explanation: The Moon is always half lit; what changes is how much of that lit half faces us. Earth's shadow only matters during a lunar eclipse.

questions.stem: Which model correctly explains the apparent movement of the Sun across the sky each day?
options: The Sun moves back and forth in the sky
Earth orbits the Sun once per day
Earth rotating eastwards makes the Sun appear to move westwards
The Sun orbits Earth once per day
questions.explanation: The apparent motion is caused by our own rotation. This is why sunrise is in the east.

questions.stem: A student says summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun. Give the best correction.
options: Seasons come from axial tilt; both hemispheres would otherwise have summer at once
The hemisphere facing the Sun is the one nearer to it
The student is correct
The Sun produces more heat in summer
questions.explanation: The decisive argument is that the hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time, which distance cannot explain.

questions.stem: Why does the timing of high tide shift by about 50 minutes each day?
options: The Moon slows down each day
Earth's rotation speeds up daily
The Sun's pull shifts the timing a little each day
The Moon moves along its orbit while Earth rotates, so Earth must turn a little further
questions.explanation: Earth needs an extra ~50 minutes to catch up with the Moon's new position, so the whole tidal pattern drifts later.

questions.stem: Why is a total solar eclipse possible at all, given the Sun is vastly larger than the Moon?
options: The Moon's orbit brings it much closer during an eclipse
The Sun is about 400 times wider but also about 400 times further away, so they appear a similar size
Sunlight is dimmed by distance, so less is needed to block it
Earth's atmosphere magnifies the Moon's disc
questions.explanation: It is a coincidence of apparent size. Angular size, not actual size, determines whether one can cover the other.

questions.stem: Which observation would most strongly support a Sun-centred model over an Earth-centred one?
options: The phases of Venus, which cannot all occur if Venus orbits Earth
The Sun rises in the east
The Moon has phases
Stars appear to move at night
questions.explanation: Galileo's observation of Venus showing a full set of phases was decisive. The other observations are explained equally well by either model.

questions.stem: Why does the Moon not always appear the same size in the sky?
options: Its orbit is slightly elliptical, so its distance from Earth varies
The Moon expands and contracts
Earth's atmosphere changes its real size
The Sun lights different amounts of it
questions.explanation: Distance variation produces the difference between a 'supermoon' and a smaller apparent disc.

questions.stem: Why are tides higher at some coasts than others even with the same Moon position?
options: Local coastline shape and ocean depth amplify or reduce the tidal range
The Moon pulls harder on some countries
Only some coasts have tides
Tides depend on air temperature
questions.explanation: The Bay of Fundy's enormous range comes from its shape and resonance, not from a stronger lunar pull there.

questions.stem: How does the tilt of Earth's axis explain why polar regions have 24-hour daylight in summer?
options: Earth stops rotating at the poles
The tilt keeps that pole in sunlight through a full rotation
The Sun is directly overhead at the poles
The poles are closest to the Sun
questions.explanation: With the pole tilted towards the Sun, rotation never carries it into darkness. The Sun stays low, not overhead.

questions.stem: A model shows the Moon orbiting Earth in the same plane as Earth's orbit. What would it wrongly predict?
options: That the Moon reflects sunlight
An eclipse every new moon and every full moon
That the Moon has phases
That the Moon takes a month to orbit
questions.explanation: The tilt is what makes eclipses rare. A flat model gets the phases right but the eclipse frequency badly wrong — useful for showing that models have limits.

questions.stem: Why does the same side of the Moon always face Earth if the Moon is rotating?
options: Earth's gravity holds one side still while the rest turns
Its rotation period exactly matches its orbital period
It rotates too slowly to notice
It does not truly rotate
questions.explanation: Tidal locking synchronises the two periods. The Moon does rotate — once per orbit.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason to describe Earth, Sun and Moon motions as 'cyclic'?
options: They follow a pattern that drifts unpredictably over centuries
They are controlled by the seasons
They repeat at regular intervals, allowing future positions to be calculated
They move in circles exactly
questions.explanation: Cyclic means repeating regularly, which is precisely what makes eclipses, tides and seasons predictable. The orbits are elliptical, not perfect circles.

questions.stem: Why can a lunar eclipse be seen by more people than a solar eclipse?
options: Lunar eclipses last longer than a whole day
The Moon is brighter during an eclipse
Solar eclipses are invisible without equipment
Earth's shadow is large and the eclipsed Moon is visible from the whole night side
questions.explanation: Anyone who can see the Moon sees the eclipse. A solar eclipse requires standing in a narrow shadow path.

questions.stem: How long is one day on Earth?
options: About 365 days
About 30 days
About 24 hours
About 12 hours
questions.explanation: One rotation on its axis takes about 24 hours.
questions.teaching:
Two different motions produce our two most basic units of time, and it is worth keeping them apart.

Earth spins on its axis, and one complete spin brings the same point back to face the Sun. That rotation is what gives us the cycle of daylight and darkness. Separately, Earth travels around the Sun, and one complete circuit is a much longer period. So one motion produces the shorter unit and the other produces the longer, and confusing which is which is the standard error in these questions.

questions.stem: What is a waxing moon?
options: A moon in eclipse
A moon whose lit portion is increasing
A moon whose lit portion is decreasing
A fully dark moon
questions.explanation: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

questions.stem: What is a waning moon?
options: A moon whose lit portion is decreasing
A moon whose lit portion is increasing
A fully lit moon
A moon in eclipse
questions.explanation: Waning follows the full moon as the lit fraction shrinks back.

questions.stem: What is an equinox?
options: A lunar eclipse
A time when day and night are of roughly equal length
The longest day of the year
The shortest day of the year
questions.explanation: Equinoxes occur around March and September; solstices are the extremes.

questions.stem: What is a solstice?
options: A day with equal day and night
The day the Moon is full
The day of an eclipse
The day with the longest or shortest daylight of the year
questions.explanation: Solstices mark the extremes of the Sun's apparent path.

questions.stem: What causes a shadow?
options: Light reflecting back off a surface
An object blocking light from a source
Light being absorbed by air
Light bending around an object
questions.explanation: Eclipses are shadows on an astronomical scale.

questions.stem: Which is larger, the Sun or Earth?
options: It varies depending on Earth's position in its orbit
The Sun, by a very large margin
Earth
Earth, by a small margin
questions.explanation: The Sun's diameter is roughly 109 times Earth's.

questions.stem: What is a low tide?
options: When the Moon is new
When there is no Moon visible
When sea level at a place is at its lowest in the tidal cycle
When the sea is calm
questions.explanation: High and low tides alternate as the Earth rotates relative to the Moon.

questions.stem: Which direction does the Sun appear to rise?
options: In the west
In the north
In the south
In the east
questions.explanation: Earth rotates eastwards, so the Sun appears to come up in the east.
questions.teaching:
Earth spins on its axis from west to east, and everything we see in the sky moves the opposite way as a result.

Because we are turning eastwards, objects appear to come up over the horizon on the eastern side, travel across the sky, and set on the western side. This applies to the Sun, the Moon and the stars alike — none of them is actually moving across the sky at that rate. Knowing the direction of Earth's spin lets you work out the apparent motion rather than memorising it.

questions.stem: Why do craters on the Moon last far longer than those on Earth?
options: The Moon has no atmosphere or liquid water to erode them
The Moon is much older
Moon rock is harder
Craters on Earth are never formed
questions.explanation: Weathering, erosion and plate tectonics erase Earth's craters over time.

questions.stem: Why does the Moon have almost no atmosphere?
options: Its gravity is too weak to hold gases
It is too cold for gases
Gases were blown away by the Sun only recently
It never had any gases
questions.explanation: Lower mass means weaker gravity, so gas molecules escape into space.

questions.stem: A student in Melbourne sees the Sun highest in the northern sky at midday. Why?
options: It is an optical illusion
Melbourne lies on the equator, so the Sun passes overhead
Melbourne is south of the tropics, so the Sun is always to the north at noon
The Sun's path shifts north during winter only
questions.explanation: From southern mid-latitudes the Sun's daily path passes through the northern sky.

questions.stem: Why does the Southern Hemisphere have Christmas in summer?
options: Earth's tilt puts the southern hemisphere towards the Sun in December
Earth is closest to the Sun in December
The Sun is stronger in December
The Southern Hemisphere rotates faster
questions.explanation: Tilt, not distance, sets the seasons — Earth is actually near its closest point to the Sun in early January.

questions.stem: How does the model of Earth, Sun and Moon explain why eclipses are relatively rare?
options: Eclipses need special weather
The Moon stops orbiting occasionally
Eclipses only happen in leap years
The three bodies must line up closely, which the Moon's tilted orbit prevents most months
questions.explanation: Alignment is the constraint, and orbital tilt makes exact alignment uncommon.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to look directly at a solar eclipse?
options: It is not dangerous
Intense sunlight can damage the retina even when partly blocked
The Moon emits harmful rays
Eclipses produce radiation from space
questions.explanation: The reduced brightness removes the instinct to look away while the damaging intensity remains.

questions.stem: Which model best explains the pattern of two tides a day?
options: Tidal bulges on opposite sides of Earth, which a place rotates through
The Moon pulling water only on one side
The Sun causing all tides alone
Wind driving water twice daily
questions.explanation: The near-side and far-side bulges mean most coasts pass through two highs per rotation.

questions.stem: Why does the Moon appear larger near the horizon even though its actual size is unchanged?
options: The Moon is genuinely closer at the horizon
Earth's shadow enlarges it
It is a perceptual illusion caused by nearby reference objects
The atmosphere magnifies it
questions.explanation: The Moon illusion is well documented and is a psychological effect, not an optical or astronomical one.

questions.stem: Why do solar and lunar eclipses not occur in the same month as each other every time?
options: Alignment conditions differ for each and depend on where the Moon crosses Earth's orbital plane
The Moon's orbit takes slightly longer than a calendar month, so the two events drift apart over time
Each eclipse uses up the alignment, so a second one cannot form until the Moon has orbited again
Solar eclipses need a new moon and lunar eclipses a full moon, which never fall in the same month
questions.explanation: Eclipses come in seasons, and whether both types occur depends on the precise geometry at each crossing.

questions.stem: Which observation supports the claim that the Moon does not produce its own light?
options: It moves across the sky
Its lit portion always faces the Sun's direction
It is visible at night
It appears white
questions.explanation: The lit side tracking the Sun's position is direct evidence of reflection.

questions.stem: Why does modelling the Earth-Sun-Moon system help make predictions?
options: Regular geometry means positions can be calculated far into the future
Models make events happen
Models remove the need for observation
Eclipse dates are recorded from past cycles rather than calculated
questions.explanation: The predictive power of the model is the strongest argument for it — eclipses are forecast decades ahead and occur on time.

questions.stem: A model shows the Moon much closer to Earth than it really is. What limitation does this create?
options: There is no limitation
It misrepresents the scale, so eclipse geometry and apparent sizes are wrong
It makes the model unusable for anything
It changes the Moon's phases
questions.explanation: Most classroom models cannot be to scale in both size and distance, which is a limitation worth stating explicitly.

questions.stem: What is an orbit?
options: The distance between two bodies
The time taken to rotate once
The curved path one body takes around another
The spinning of a body on its axis
questions.explanation: Rotation is spinning on an axis; revolution is orbiting.

questions.stem: What is rotation?
options: The pull of gravity
The spinning of a body about its own axis
The path around another body
The tilt of an axis
questions.explanation: Earth's rotation gives day and night; its orbit gives the year.

questions.stem: What keeps planets in orbit around the Sun?
options: The solar wind
Gravity
Magnetism
Air pressure
questions.explanation: The Sun's gravitational pull continually curves each planet's path.
questions.teaching:
An orbit needs two things: sideways motion, and a force pulling the object towards what it orbits.

The force is the mutual attraction between masses, which grows with mass and weakens with distance. A planet is moving fast enough sideways that the pull bends its path into a curve rather than dragging it straight in — effectively it keeps falling and keeps missing. Magnetism is the tempting alternative because the Sun has a strong magnetic field, but planets are not magnets, and the same arrangement holds moons around planets.

questions.stem: What is a satellite?
options: An object in orbit around a larger body
A body that generates its own light
A body that orbits the Sun directly
Any object launched into space
questions.explanation: The Moon is Earth's natural satellite; others are artificial.

questions.stem: What is the term for the Moon's shape appearing to change?
options: Orbits
Tides
Phases
Eclipses
questions.explanation: Phases result from the changing viewing angle of the Moon's lit half.
questions.teaching:
The Moon does not produce light; it reflects sunlight, and half of it is lit at any moment.

What changes is how much of that lit half we can see from Earth, which depends on where the Moon is in its orbit. When it sits between Earth and the Sun, the lit side faces away from us. When Earth sits between them, we see the lit side fully. In between we see part of it. The cycle takes about a month and the sequence has a collective name, with individual stages called new, crescent, quarter, gibbous and full.

questions.stem: What is a total solar eclipse?
options: When the Sun is only partly covered
When the Moon is fully lit
When the Moon completely covers the Sun's disc as seen from a place on Earth
When Earth blocks all sunlight to the Moon
questions.explanation: Totality is visible only within the narrow path of the Moon's full shadow.

questions.stem: What is the term for the shortest day of the year?
options: An equinox
A lunar eclipse
The winter solstice
The summer solstice
questions.explanation: The winter solstice has the least daylight for that hemisphere.

questions.stem: How does the Moon affect the oceans?
options: It heats the ocean surface
It creates ocean currents directly
Its magnetic field pulls on the dissolved salt in seawater
Its gravity produces tidal bulges that cause tides
questions.explanation: The Sun contributes as well, but the Moon's effect is roughly twice as strong.

questions.stem: Why does the Sun appear to move across the sky during the day?
options: The atmosphere bends the light
Earth rotates on its axis
The Sun orbits Earth
Earth orbits the Sun daily
questions.explanation: The apparent motion mirrors our own rotation.

questions.stem: Why is the Moon visible during the day sometimes?
options: It is above the horizon and bright enough to see against the daytime sky
It reflects sunlight more strongly when the Sun is high
It is only visible in the hours just after sunrise
Sunlight reflects off Earth onto the Moon during the day
questions.explanation: Its position relative to the Sun determines when it is up, not whether it is day or night.

questions.stem: Why does the length of daylight vary more at higher latitudes?
options: Daylight is constant everywhere
The tilt has a greater effect the further you are from the equator
The Sun is closer at high latitudes
The atmosphere is thinner there
questions.explanation: Near the equator day length changes little; near the poles it varies from continuous day to continuous night.

questions.stem: A model uses a torch, a large ball and a small ball. What does the torch represent?
options: The Sun
Earth
The Moon
A star cluster
questions.explanation: The light source models the Sun, which illuminates the other two bodies.

questions.stem: Why can the Moon appear reddish during a total lunar eclipse?
options: The Moon emits red light
Earth's atmosphere bends and filters sunlight into the shadow
The Moon heats up and glows
Mars reflects onto the Moon
questions.explanation: Longer wavelengths scatter less and reach the Moon, giving the blood moon effect.

questions.stem: Why do tides occur roughly twice daily rather than once?
options: Earth rotates twice a day
Tides are caused by the Sun alone
Bulges form on both the near and far sides of Earth
The Moon orbits twice a day
questions.explanation: Earth rotates through both bulges in roughly one day.

questions.stem: Why is the statement 'the Moon has a dark side' misleading?
options: The far side is lit constantly while the near side passes through night
The Moon turns too slowly for sunlight to reach the far side during its orbit
The far side sits in Earth's shadow all month, which is what causes the phases
Every part of the Moon receives sunlight during its cycle; the far side is simply never visible from Earth
questions.explanation: 'Far side' is accurate; 'dark side' confuses visibility with illumination.
